key_terms.meaning: A body in which the distance between any two points never changes; it can still move as a whole
Motion in which every point of the body has the same velocity and the same acceleration at a given instant
Motion in which every point of the body travels on a circle centred on one fixed line, the axis of rotation
The fixed line about which a body in fixed-axis rotation turns; points on it have zero velocity
θ, the angle turned by the body, measured in radians (1 rev = 2π rad)
ω = dθ/dt, the rate of turning, in rad/s; every point of the body shares the same ω
α = dω/dt = d²θ/dt², in rad/s²; the rate at which ω changes
Motion in which all points stay in parallel planes and the body both translates and rotates
v_B = v_A + ω × r_B/A for two points A and B on the same rigid body
a_B = a_A + α × r_B/A − ω² r_B/A, the last term being the centripetal part
The point IC about which the body appears to rotate purely at one instant; its velocity is zero at that instant
I_G = Σ mᵢ rᵢ² about an axis through the mass centre G, in kg·m²
k with I = m k², the distance at which the whole mass could sit to give the same I

key_terms.term: Equation of motion for plane motion
key_terms.meaning: ΣF = m a_G and ΣM_G = I_G α, taken together for the same body

key_terms.term: Angular momentum of a rigid body
key_terms.meaning: H_G = I_G ω about the mass centre for plane motion, in kg·m²/s
∫M dt, the moment of a force integrated over time; it equals the change in angular momentum

key_terms.term: Work-energy principle for a rigid body
key_terms.meaning: U = Δ(½ m v_G² + ½ I_G ω²): work by forces and moments equals the change in kinetic energy
Oscillation of the form x = A sin(ω_n t + φ), with acceleration proportional to −x
ω_n = √(k/m) rad/s for a spring-mass system; f_n = ω_n/2π in Hz

takeaways: Any rigid-body motion can be built from translation of a chosen base point plus rotation about that point.
In fixed-axis rotation every point has the same ω and α, but linear speed grows with distance from the axis as v = ωr.
The relative velocity equation v_B = v_A + ω × r_B/A solves planar velocity problems with one vector triangle.
The relative acceleration equation carries an extra centripetal term ω²r, which points from B towards A.
The instantaneous centre turns a general plane-motion velocity problem into a pure-rotation problem about a point with zero velocity.
For plane kinetics use ΣF = m a_G and ΣM_G = I_G α together; forces alone never fix the rotation.
Angular momentum about G is simply I_G ω, so angular impulse changes spin exactly as linear impulse changes linear momentum.
Work-energy is the fast route when you know displacements but not time; impulse-momentum is the fast route when you know time or a collision.
A spring-mass system oscillates with ω_n = √(k/m), fixed by stiffness and mass alone and not by the starting pull.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit almost always ask you to draw the free-body and kinetic diagrams first, then combine force and moment equations or a velocity/acceleration diagram with clear vector directions.

bank.q: Distinguish translation, fixed-axis rotation and general plane motion of a rigid body, giving one practical example of each and stating which quantities are common to all points of the body in each case.
outline: Translation: all points share v and a; example of a lift cage or a drawer
Fixed-axis rotation: points move on circles about one fixed line; ω and α common to all points, v = ωr varies with r; example of a door or a fan blade
General plane motion: translation of a base point plus rotation about it; example of a rolling wheel or a connecting rod
State that a rigid body has 3 degrees of freedom in plane motion (two translations and one rotation)

bank.q: Define angular displacement, angular velocity and angular acceleration for a body rotating about a fixed axis, and write the three kinematic equations for constant angular acceleration.
outline: θ in radians, ω = dθ/dt in rad/s, α = dω/dt in rad/s²
Equations: ω = ω₀ + αt, θ = ω₀t + ½αt², ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ
State the condition: α constant only
Note 1 rev = 2π rad and units must be consistent

bank.q: Explain why the mass moment of inertia of a rigid body depends on the axis chosen, and state the parallel-axis theorem.
outline: I = Σ mᵢ rᵢ², so I grows with the square of the distance of mass from the axis
I_G about the mass centre is the smallest for parallel axes
Parallel-axis theorem: I = I_G + m d², with d the distance between the axes
Radius of gyration k with I = m k²
Give a worked value for a standard shape such as a disc about its centre

bank.q: State Newton's second law for plane motion of a rigid body and explain why a single force equation is not enough to describe the motion.
outline: ΣF = m a_G, the resultant force sets the mass-centre acceleration
ΣM_G = I_G α, the resultant moment about G sets the angular acceleration
A force applied off-centre produces both translation and rotation
Both equations must be written for the same body and the same instant
Mention the free-body diagram and the kinetic (inertia) diagram

bank.q: A wheel of radius 0.4 m starts from rest and has a constant angular acceleration of 3 rad/s². Find its angular velocity after 5 s, the number of revolutions turned, and the tangential and normal accelerations of a point on the rim at that instant.
outline: ω = ω₀ + αt = 0 + 3 × 5 = 15 rad/s
a_n = ω²r = 225 × 0.4 = 90 m/s² directed towards the centre
Total acceleration magnitude √(1.2² + 90²) ≈ 90 m/s²

bank.q: A 5 m ladder rests with its foot on the floor and its top against a wall. The foot slides away from the wall at a constant 1.5 m/s. Using the instantaneous centre of rotation, find the angular velocity of the ladder and the speed of the top end when the ladder makes 30° with the floor.
outline: Velocity of the foot is horizontal, velocity of the top is vertical
IC lies where the perpendiculars to these two velocities meet: at the corner point (x, y)
At 30°, height of top y = 5 sin 30° = 2.5 m and base distance x = 5 cos 30° = 4.33 m
ω = v_foot / y = 1.5 / 2.5 = 0.6 rad/s
v_top = ω x = 0.6 × 4.33 ≈ 2.6 m/s, directed down the wall
Check with the relative velocity equation as a cross-check

bank.q: A uniform disc of mass 20 kg and radius 0.5 m rotates about its central axis. A constant braking moment of 25 N·m acts on it. If it spins at 40 rad/s, find the time to stop and the number of turns made.
outline: Time t = ω/|α| = 40/10 = 4 s
Alternative: angular impulse–momentum M t = I ω gives the same time

bank.q: A pulley of moment of inertia 0.5 kg·m² and radius 0.2 m carries a light cord with a 2 kg mass hanging from it. Find the angular acceleration of the pulley and the tension in the cord. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
outline: Free-body diagrams for the mass and for the pulley separately
For the mass: m g − T = m a with a = α r
For the pulley: T r = I α
T = I α / r = 16.9 N, which is less than the weight of 19.6 N
Note that the tension is not equal to the weight because the mass is accelerating

bank.q: A flywheel of moment of inertia 10 kg·m² is brought from rest to 20 rad/s. Find the work done, and then find how long a 50 N·m driving moment must act to produce this speed from rest.
outline: Work done = change in kinetic energy = ½ I ω² = 0.5 × 10 × 400 = 2000 J
Angular impulse = M t = I ω → t = 10 × 20 / 50 = 4 s
Average power = work/time = 2000/4 = 500 W
State which principle is used and why the other would also work here

bank.q: Two points A and B on a rigid link are in plane motion. Starting from the position vector relation r_B = r_A + r_B/A, derive the relative velocity and relative acceleration equations, and identify which term is directed from B towards A.
outline: Differentiate r_B = r_A + r_B/A to get v_B = v_A + ω × r_B/A
Differentiate again: a_B = a_A + α × r_B/A + ω × (ω × r_B/A)
The last term equals −ω² r_B/A, magnitude ω² r_B/A, directed from B towards A
Call it the centripetal or normal component; the α term is the tangential component
Use the result to explain why two points on a rigid body can never have velocities along the line joining them that differ

bank.q: Explain the instantaneous centre of rotation method for velocity analysis of a rigid body in plane motion. State how the IC is located for a rolling wheel without slip and for a sliding ladder, and give one case where the method fails.
outline: At one instant the velocity field is the same as pure rotation about the IC, so v = ω × r from the IC
IC found from two known velocity directions: draw perpendiculars at the two points
Rolling wheel without slipping: IC is the contact point with the ground
Sliding ladder: IC is the corner where the two perpendiculars meet
Limitation: acceleration cannot be found from the IC directly, and the IC moves with time; when the two perpendiculars are parallel, the IC is at infinity and ω = 0 at that instant

bank.q: Compare the work-energy method, the impulse-momentum method and the direct use of Newton's second law for a rigid body in plane motion. For a flywheel being braked to rest, say which method you would choose and why.
outline: Work-energy: relates force/moment to speed and displacement; best when time is not asked
Impulse-momentum: relates force/moment to speed and time; best when time or impact is involved
Newton's second law with I_G α: gives accelerations at an instant and also the internal reactions
For braking a flywheel: angular impulse–momentum gives the stopping time in one line; work-energy gives the angle turned
State the assumptions behind each and note that all three must agree

bank.q: A mass of 2 kg hangs on a spring of stiffness 800 N/m. Set up the equation of motion, prove that the motion is simple harmonic, and find the natural frequency and periodic time. Discuss what changes if the mass is doubled.
outline: Static deflection takes up the weight; measure x from the static equilibrium position
Equation of motion: m ẍ = −k x, so ẍ + (k/m) x = 0
This is simple harmonic motion with ω_n = √(k/m) = √400 = 20 rad/s
f_n = ω_n/2π ≈ 3.18 Hz and T = 1/f_n ≈ 0.314 s
Doubling m gives ω_n = √(k/2m) = 14.14 rad/s, a lower frequency and longer period; the amplitude depends only on the initial pull

bank.q: A uniform cylinder rolls down an incline without slipping. Using both the force–moment equations and the work-energy principle, obtain its acceleration along the incline, and explain why it is smaller than g sinθ.
outline: Forces: m g sinθ down the slope, friction f up the slope, normal reaction N
Translation: m g sinθ − f = m a; rotation: f r = I_G α with a = α r
For a cylinder I_G = ½ m r², giving a = (2/3) g sinθ
Work-energy check: m g h = ½ m v² + ½ I_G ω² leads to the same v
Part of the available energy goes into spin, so the linear acceleration is less than g sinθ; without friction the body would slide with a = g sinθ

glossary.def: An ideal body whose points keep fixed distances from one another, so it cannot stretch or bend.
Motion in which every point of the body stays in a plane parallel to one fixed plane.
Motion in which every point of the body has the same velocity and acceleration at any instant.
Rotation in which one line of the body stays fixed in space and all other points move on circles about it.
The angle θ turned by a rotating body, measured in radians.
ω = dθ/dt, the time rate of turning, in rad/s.
α = dω/dt, the time rate of change of angular velocity, in rad/s².
a_t = α r, the part of a point's acceleration along its circular path.
a_n = ω² r, the part of a point's acceleration directed towards the centre of its circle.
Motion that is neither pure translation nor pure rotation, but translation of a base point plus rotation about it.
Solving velocity problems with v_B = v_A + ω × r_B/A, usually by a vector triangle or polygon.
Solving acceleration problems with a_B = a_A + α × r_B/A − ω² r_B/A.
The point about which the body appears to rotate at one instant, having zero velocity at that instant.
The locus traced by the instantaneous centre as the motion proceeds.
The point G where the resultant of the distributed weights acts and about which ΣF = m a_G holds.
I = Σ mᵢ rᵢ², a body's resistance to angular acceleration about a chosen axis, in kg·m².
k = √(I/m), the distance from the axis at which the whole mass could be placed to give the same I.
I = I_G + m d², giving I about any axis a distance d from a parallel axis through the mass centre.
H_G = I_G ω about the mass centre for plane motion, in kg·m²/s.
The time integral ∫M dt of a moment; it equals the change in angular momentum.
½ I_G ω², the energy held in a body's spin about its mass centre.
Oscillation with acceleration proportional to displacement and directed towards the mean position.
The frequency at which a system oscillates freely once disturbed; ω_n = √(k/m) for a spring-mass system.
k, the restoring force per unit displacement of a spring, in N/m.
T = 2π/ω_n, the time taken for one complete oscillation, in seconds.
